title: Operations on irrational numbers
competency: Multiply, divide, add and subtract irrational numbers, using the product and quotient rules and like radicals.

keywords.def: The number under the radical sign: 5 in √5.
Radicals with the same index and the same radicand, such as 2√5 and 7√5. Only like radicals can be added.
A decimal that neither ends nor repeats, such as √2 or π.

en.text: For positive a and b, √a × √b = √(ab) and √a ÷ √b = √(a/b). So √2 × √3 = √6. A product of two irrational numbers may be rational: √2 × √2 = 2. Also a√b = √(a²b). So 3√2 = √18, and √50 = 5√2.

am.text: a እና b አዎንታዊ ሲሆኑ √a × √b = √(ab) እና √a ÷ √b = √(a/b) ነው። ስለዚህ √2 × √3 = √6። የሁለት ኢ-ምክንያታዊ ቁጥሮች ብዜት ምክንያታዊ ሊሆን ይችላል፤ √2 × √2 = 2። ደግሞ a√b = √(a²b) ነው። ስለዚህ 3√2 = √18 እና √50 = 5√2።

screens.title: Irrational times irrational
screens.text: √2 is irrational. √3 and √8 are irrational too.
screens.ask: Is the product of two irrational numbers always irrational? Guess.
screens.after:
Good guesses say "sometimes".
√2 × √3 = √6 is irrational.
But √2 × √2 = 2 and √2 × √8 = 4 are rational.
Try them below, then read on.

screens.title: Activity 1.11: what happens?
paras: 1 + √2 is irrational. A rational number plus an irrational number is irrational.
So a product of two irrational numbers is not always irrational.

screens.title: Try the products
screens.ask: Tap each product. Is the answer rational or irrational?

screens.title: The product rule
screens.note: In Example 1(c) the printed book is missing a plus sign: "(√2 × 1)(√2 × √5)" should read (√2 × 1) + (√2 × √5).

screens.title: Name it
defs: The number under the radical sign. In √a × √b = √(ab), the radicands multiply.

screens.title: Use the product rule
screens.why:
Product rule: √a × √b = √(ab).
Multiply the radicands: 3 × 5 = 15.
So √3 × √5 = √15.
√8 is a slip: it adds 3 + 5 instead of multiplying.
screens.clue: Multiply the radicands and keep one √.

screens.title: The quotient rule
screens.note: The quotient may be rational or irrational.

screens.title: Moving a number inside the root
paras: If a > 0 and b > 0, then a√b = √(a²b) and √(a²b) = a√b.

screens.title: Write √50 as a√b
screens.text: Find the largest perfect square that divides the radicand.

screens.title: Find the square inside 50
screens.intro: Tap ▶. Look for a pair of equal primes.
say: 50 = 2 × 25. 2 is prime, so it is a leaf.

50 = 2 × 5 × 5. The pair 5 × 5 = 25 is a perfect square.
√50 = √(5 × 5) × √2 = 5√2.

screens.title: Simplest a√b form
screens.text: Simplify the root: write √50 in the form a√b, with b as small as possible.
screens.why:
Find the largest perfect square that divides 50: it is 25.
50 = 25 × 2.
√50 = √25 × √2 = 5 × √2.
So √50 = 5√2.
25√2 forgets to take the root of 25.
screens.clue: Find the largest perfect square that divides 50.

screens.title: Quotient rule
screens.why:
Quotient rule: √a ÷ √b = √(a ÷ b).
27 ÷ 3 = 9, so √27 ÷ √3 = √9.
√9 = 3, because 3 × 3 = 9.
Answer: 3.

screens.title: A square classroom
screens.text: A classroom floor in Gondar is a square. Its side is 3√2 m.
screens.why:
Area of a square = side × side.
(3√2)² = 3√2 × 3√2.
Multiply the whole numbers: 3 × 3 = 9.
Multiply the roots: √2 × √2 = 2.
9 × 2 = 18, so the area is 18 m².
screens.clue: Area = side × side. Write 3√2 as √18 first.

en.text: The sum or difference of two irrational numbers may be rational or irrational. Like radicals have the same radicand, such as 2√3 and 4√3. Add them like like terms: 2√3 + 4√3 = 6√3. First simplify each root, so √8 + √2 becomes 2√2 + √2 = 3√2.

am.text: የሁለት ኢ-ምክንያታዊ ቁጥሮች ድምር ወይም ልዩነት ምክንያታዊ ወይም ኢ-ምክንያታዊ ሊሆን ይችላል። ተመሳሳይ ሥሮች አንድ አይነት ከሥር ያለ ቁጥር አላቸው፤ ለምሳሌ 2√3 እና 4√3። እንደ ተመሳሳይ ተርሞች ደምራቸው፤ 2√3 + 4√3 = 6√3። መጀመሪያ እያንዳንዱን ሥር አቅልል፤ √8 + √2 = 2√2 + √2 = 3√2 ይሆናል።

screens.title: Does √2 + √3 equal √5?
screens.text: Many students write √2 + √3 = √5. Use your calculator: √2 ≈ 1.414 and √3 ≈ 1.732.
screens.after:
No. √2 + √3 ≈ 1.414 + 1.732 = 3.146.
But √5 ≈ 2.236.
"Only roughly" is not right either: 3.15 and 2.24 are far apart.
Read on to see which roots can be added.

screens.title: Can roots be added?
screens.note: Move the sliders. √a + √b is always bigger than √(a + b). So √2 + √3 ≠ √5.

screens.title: Name it
defs: Radicals with the same radicand, such as 2√3 and 4√3. Only like radicals can be added into one radical.

screens.title: Why not one radical?
screens.text: Like radicals: why can't √2 + √3 be written as one radical?
screens.why:
Like radicals have the same radicand.
√2 has radicand 2 and √3 has radicand 3. They are not alike.
So they cannot be joined into one root.
Check: √2 + √3 ≈ 3.146, but √5 ≈ 2.236 and √6 ≈ 2.449.
So "√2 + √3 = √5" and "= √6" are both wrong.

screens.title: Example 2: like radicals
paras: Like radicals add like like terms.

screens.title: Simplify first
screens.text: First write each √(a²b) as a√b. Then add or subtract like radicals.

screens.title: A correction
screens.note: Correction: Example 3(d) in the printed book ends "6√2 − 2√2 = 8√2". The correct answer is 4√2.

screens.title: Find the like radicals
screens.text: Simplify each root. Is it a multiple of √2 or of √3?
screens.why:
Take out the largest perfect square each time.
8, 18 and 50 are 4 × 2, 9 × 2 and 25 × 2: multiples of √2.
12, 27 and 75 are 4 × 3, 9 × 3 and 25 × 3: multiples of √3.
Only roots in the same group can be added.
screens.clue: Look for 4, 9 or 25 inside each number.

screens.title: Simplify, then add
screens.text: Simplify each root, then add like radicals: √12 + √27 = ?
screens.why:
√12 = √(4 × 3) = 2√3.
√27 = √(9 × 3) = 3√3.
Now they are like radicals: 2√3 + 3√3 = (2 + 3)√3.
So √12 + √27 = 5√3.
√39 is wrong: roots do not add under one sign.
screens.clue: Simplify each radical first so they become like radicals.

screens.title: Subtract like radicals
screens.why:
Both terms have √5, so they are like radicals.
Subtract the numbers in front: 2 − 4 = −2.
So 2√5 − 4√5 = −2√5.

screens.title: Fencing two plots
screens.text: Two square gardens in Mekelle have sides √8 m and √18 m. Tsegaye walks one side of each.
screens.ask: Simplify and add: he walks √8 + √18 = ___√2 m.
screens.clue: Write each root as a√2 first.

items.why:
Keep the number in front: 2.
Multiply the roots: √5 × √7 = √35.
So 2√5 × √7 = 2√35.
√70 is wrong: the 2 is outside the root, so it does not go under it.

−√2 × √6 = −√(2 × 6) = −√12.
12 = 4 × 3 and √4 = 2.
So −√12 = −2√3.
The sign stays negative: minus times plus is minus.

Multiply the tops: 1 × 10 = 10.
Multiply the bottoms: √5 × √5 = 5.
10/5 = 2.
The product is 2, a rational number.

items.clue: Use the distributive law. The √3 terms cancel.

items.text: 2(a) Always, sometimes or never true? "The product of two irrational numbers is rational."
items.why:
Test examples.
√2 × √2 = 2: rational.
√2 × √3 = √6: irrational.
We found one of each, so it is sometimes true.

Keep the minus sign in front.
√15/√3 = √(15 ÷ 3) = √5.
So −√15/√3 = −√5.

items.ask: 2(a) Move the number inside the root: 4√2 = √___
items.why:
Rule: a√b = √(a² × b).
Square the number in front: 4² = 16.
Multiply: 16 × 2 = 32.
So 4√2 = √32.

items.ask: 2(b) Move the number inside the root: 5√3 = √___
2(d) Move the number inside the root: 7√6 = √___

items.why:
√3 means 1√3.
Both terms have √3, so add the numbers in front: 1 + 4 = 5.
So √3 + 4√3 = 5√3.

items.ask: (j) Add the decimals; write the sum as a fraction: 2.1010010001… + 1.0101101110… = ___
items.why:
Add the whole parts: 2 + 1 = 3.
Add the decimals place by place: each place has one 1 and one 0.
So every decimal digit of the sum is 1: 3.111…
0.111… = 1/9, so the sum is 3 + 1/9 = 28/9.
Two irrational numbers gave a rational sum.
items.clue: Add digit by digit. What repeats?

test.why:
√2 × √8 = √(2 × 8) = √16.
√16 = 4, because 4 × 4 = 16.
So the product is 4, a rational number.

screens.title: Spot a perfect square factor
steps: Take 12. Which perfect square divides it? 4 does: 12 = 4 × 3.

screens.title: Your turn
screens.why:
Try each one: 18 ÷ 9 = 2 exactly, and 9 = 3².
18 ÷ 4 = 4.5 and 18 ÷ 16 is not whole.
6 divides 18, but 6 is not a perfect square.
So the answer is 9, and √18 = 3√2.
screens.clue: Try 4, 9 and 16. Which one divides 18 exactly?
